newsitem.title: INDIA: India says no to scrapping of hazardous U.S. ships.
newsitem.headline: India says no to scrapping of hazardous U.S. ships.

text.p: India said on Tuesday it would not become a dumping ground for dangerous waste and would not permit the dismantling on its shores of two American ships which had carried hazardous materials.
"India will not be allowed to become a dumping ground," Environment Minister Saifuddin Soz told the lower house of parliament, the Lok Sabha.
India's western state of Gujarat has the biggest shipbreaking industry in Asia where about 90 percent of the region's vessels are dismantled and sold as scrap.

Soz, an outspoken critic of the West's environmental commitments, said a request by the United States embassy to sell two American vessels for break-up in India had been turned down for environmental reasons.
He said the likely presence of dangerous materials on the ships could affect the country's fauna and flora and they would not be scrapped in India until they had been checked for dangerous materials.
He did not specify what materials the ships had carried.

"The Ministry of Environment felt the ships could not be sold for breaking in India till an assessment had been made about the quantity of hazardous material present in such ships," he told the Lok Sabha.
An American embassy official said they had taken up the issue of the sale of such ships with the Environment Ministry but had not yet received a reply.
As for the two ships in question, the official said they were trying to trace their whereabouts.
They had yet to find out whether the owners of the two ships had got permission for them to leave U.S. shores in line with regulations concerning the movement of such ships, the official said.
However, Soz later said the ships had probably already entered Indian waters off the state of Gujarat.

"Last night the Gujarat maritime board reported that these two ships or other ships might have entered the Gujarat coast," Soz said, adding that the relaxing of import laws since 1991 had made ships' entry easier but not guaranteed.
"With the liberalisation there is an open general licence and any party can bring in a ship, but they have to fulfil the conditions laid down by the Ministry of Environment and Forests."
